stem: Fraud scores must be computed on each transaction as it happens, within 100ms. This calls for:
options: A synchronous real-time serving endpoint that scores each request
A daily export of scored transactions delivered to the risk team
A weekly notebook run that recomputes scores for all accounts
A nightly batch job that writes scores to a table for later lookup
rationale: A per-event decision with a sub-second budget requires synchronous online inference; every batch or scheduled option delivers scores long after the transaction is gone.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Confuses analytical reporting delivery with operational, in-the-loop scoring
Treats ad-hoc notebook execution as a substitute for a running service
Assumes precomputed batch scores can cover events that have not happened yet

stem: A recommender must score all 50M users once per day to populate a cache that is read at page load. This is best served by:
options: An analyst exporting scores from a notebook each morning by hand
A streaming pipeline that scores each user on every click event
A real-time endpoint invoked once per user request at page load
A scheduled batch inference job that scores all users overnight
rationale: Bulk, scheduled, latency-tolerant scoring of a fixed population is the canonical batch inference case; the cache is filled ahead of time, so no per-request serving is needed.
misconceptions: Treats a manual, unrepeatable human step as a production pipeline
Confuses event-driven streaming with a fixed daily full-population refresh
Reaches for online serving even when the workload is bulk and offline
CORRECT

stem: You want to test a new model on genuine production traffic without its predictions ever affecting users. The right technique is:
options: A/B test: split users between the models and compare business metrics
Canary release: route a small share of real users to the new model
Shadow mode: mirror live traffic to the new model, discard its output
Blue-green switch: cut all traffic over to the new model in one step
rationale: Shadow (mirrored) deployment is the only listed pattern where the candidate model sees real traffic while its predictions are never returned to any user.
misconceptions: Overlooks that an A/B test deliberately serves the new model to a user arm
Overlooks that a canary still serves real users, so predictions do affect them
CORRECT
Overlooks that a blue-green cutover exposes 100% of users to the new model

stem: The main benefit of containerizing an ML service is that:
options: It compresses the model weights so the service uses less GPU memory
It removes the need for servers by running the model in the browser
It encrypts the application and its data while the container is running
It packages code, dependencies, and environment for consistent runs
rationale: A container image bundles the application with its dependency and OS-library environment, so the same artifact behaves identically across laptops, CI, and production.
misconceptions: Confuses containerization with model compression techniques like quantization
Assumes containers are serverless and eliminate the underlying compute host
Assumes a container is a security boundary that encrypts workloads by default
CORRECT

stem: Image rebuilds take 10 minutes because all dependencies reinstall on every small code change. The fix is:
options: Copy the whole application directory first, then install the dependencies
Copy the dependency manifest and install packages before copying app code
Add a fresh build timestamp label near the top of the Dockerfile
Combine every instruction into a single RUN layer to shrink the image
rationale: Layer caching invalidates every layer after the first changed one, so installing dependencies before copying frequently-edited source keeps the expensive install layer cached.
misconceptions: Gets the layer order backwards, so any code edit busts the install layer
CORRECT
Guarantees a cache miss on the very first layer, rebuilding everything
Confuses image size optimization with build-time cache reuse

stem: A production image is 6GB because it carries compilers and training libraries. The most effective remedy is:
options: Rebuild the image on a larger base distribution to consolidate layers
Use a multi-stage build so only runtime artifacts land in the final image
Mount the training libraries from a volume at container start-up instead
Delete the build tools in a later RUN step within the same Dockerfile
rationale: Multi-stage builds compile in a throwaway stage and copy only the needed artifacts forward, so build tooling never enters the shipped image's layer history.
misconceptions: Confuses base image choice with removing build tooling from the image
CORRECT
Reintroduces the environment drift that containerization exists to remove
Misses that deleting files in a later layer leaves them in earlier layers

stem: In a CI/CD pipeline for an ML service, a sound practice on each commit is to:
options: Deploy the new container straight to production and watch the error rate
Retrain the model on a developer machine and upload the new weights
Merge to main and rely on the nightly manual QA pass to catch problems
Run automated tests and linting, build the image, then deploy to staging
rationale: Automated checks, a reproducible build, and promotion through staging give fast feedback and keep unverified changes out of production.
misconceptions: Removes every gate, so defects reach users before any check has run
Reintroduces an unreproducible manual step outside the pipeline
Defers verification by a day and depends on humans rather than automation
CORRECT

stem: What makes CI/CD for ML genuinely different from CI/CD for traditional software?
options: Data and models must also be versioned and validated, not only the code
Deployment must be blocked until training loss reaches a fixed threshold
ML services cannot be tested automatically, so gates must be manual reviews
Model artifacts are just code, so ordinary unit tests cover the whole risk
rationale: ML systems have three changing inputs — code, data, and model — so the pipeline must version and validate datasets and model artifacts, not just run code tests.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Mistakes an arbitrary training metric target for the difference in kind
Denies that data validation and model evaluation can be automated at all
Ignores that a model's behaviour depends on data the code tests never see

stem: Your pipeline auto-promotes a retrained model whenever it beats the incumbent on a fixed holdout set, yet live quality drifts down over months. The most likely flaw is:
options: Retraining runs too frequently, so the weights progressively overfit noise
The holdout set is stale, so gains on it no longer reflect live traffic
Accuracy is computed inside the training image, not the serving image
The incumbent model was never given a version tag in the model registry
rationale: A frozen holdout drifts away from the live distribution, so it stops being a valid proxy — and repeated selection against it also overfits the gate itself.
misconceptions: Assumes retraining frequency alone degrades weights, independent of the gate
CORRECT
Names a real skew risk that would not produce a slow multi-month decline
Confuses a registry bookkeeping gap with an invalid evaluation gate

stem: The primary purpose of an experiment-tracking tool in an ML workflow is to:
options: Store and label raw training data as the team's system of record
Log and compare runs — params, metrics, artifacts — for reproducibility
Tune hyperparameters automatically by searching a configured space
Serve the trained model behind a low-latency authenticated HTTP endpoint
rationale: Experiment tracking records the inputs and outputs of each run so results can be compared and reproduced later; it is a record-keeping layer, not a serving, storage, or search engine.
misconceptions: Confuses run metadata tracking with a data warehouse or labelling platform
CORRECT
Confuses recording experiments with orchestrating a hyperparameter search
Confuses the tracking layer with the model serving layer

stem: Why keep versioned models in a model registry?
options: To make the deployed model load faster by caching its weights on disk
To version the training code, since the artifacts themselves never change
To improve accuracy automatically as each new version gets registered
To know which model is live, enable rollback, and trace lineage
rationale: A registry gives each artifact an identity so you can tell what is deployed, revert to a known-good version, and link it back to the data and code that produced it.
misconceptions: Confuses artifact governance with a runtime performance optimization
Assumes only code needs versions and that model artifacts are immutable
Assumes versioning itself improves a model rather than tracking it
CORRECT

stem: A teammate reruns your training script at the same Git commit but gets noticeably different metrics. Which omission best explains it?
options: The model artifact was not registered in the registry after training ended
The metrics were logged under a different experiment name in the tracker
The dataset snapshot and random seed were never pinned alongside the code
The tracking server wrote the run artifacts into a different storage bucket
rationale: Pinning the commit fixes only the code; without a pinned dataset version and seed, the data and the stochastic path both change, so the metrics legitimately differ.
misconceptions: Confuses post-training artifact promotion with training-time reproducibility
Confuses where results are filed with what actually produced the results
CORRECT
Confuses artifact storage location with the determinism of the run itself

stem: Which set of signals matters most to monitor for a deployed ML or LLM service?
options: Repository size, commit count, and the number of open pull requests
Training-set accuracy recorded at the end of the last training run
Latency, error rate, throughput, plus input drift and output quality
Hardware purchase cost, licence expiry, and the vendor's support tier
rationale: Production monitoring must cover both operational health (latency, errors, throughput) and model health (input drift, output quality), since either can fail independently.
misconceptions: Confuses repository activity metrics with runtime service behaviour
Mistakes a frozen offline training number for live production health
CORRECT
Confuses procurement and contract facts with service observability

stem: Production accuracy decays over months although input feature distributions look unchanged. The most likely cause is:
options: Training-serving skew — features are computed differently at serve time
Label leakage — a target-derived feature inflated the original scores
Data drift — the distribution of the input features has shifted over time
Concept drift — the input-to-target relationship itself has changed
rationale: When inputs are stable but performance falls, the mapping from inputs to the target has changed; that is concept drift by definition.
misconceptions: Names a real failure that would show up at launch, not as slow monthly decay
Names a training-time defect that would have shown poor accuracy from day one
Ignores the stated evidence that the input distribution has not shifted
CORRECT

stem: Mean request latency for your service sits flat at 80ms, yet users report frequent timeouts. What should you inspect first?
options: Total request throughput, since heavier traffic must mean slower replies
The mean latency over a longer rolling window to get a stabler figure
Tail latency percentiles such as p95 and p99, which an average conceals
The model's offline accuracy, since weak quality lengthens each response
rationale: Averages hide the slow minority of requests that actually time out; tail percentiles expose the distribution's right edge where the user-visible failures live.
misconceptions: Assumes throughput implies latency and still gives no view of the tail
Doubles down on the aggregate statistic that is already hiding the problem
CORRECT
Confuses a model quality metric with a request-latency distribution issue

stem: Inference traffic is spiky and unpredictable, and you do not want to pay for idle capacity. A reasonable choice is:
options: One always-on large VM sized for the highest spike you have observed
A fixed pool of small VMs with a queue absorbing every traffic burst
Manually resizing the existing VM whenever a spike gets reported to you
Autoscaling compute that adds and removes replicas as demand changes
rationale: Autoscaling matches provisioned capacity to actual demand, so spikes are absorbed while idle periods do not incur the cost of peak-sized capacity.
misconceptions: Pays for peak capacity continuously, which is exactly the stated problem
Still provisions a fixed pool that idles, and queueing only defers the load
Relies on human reaction time, which cannot track unpredictable spikes
CORRECT

stem: You must store 10TB of training images cheaply and read them from many training jobs. The best fit is:
options: A block volume attached to a single training VM's local filesystem
Object storage, which holds large files cheaply and scales elastically
An in-memory cache cluster sized to hold the entire dataset
A relational database, keeping each image inside a text column per row
rationale: Object storage is the standard cheap, elastic, network-accessible home for large immutable blobs that many jobs read.
misconceptions: Ties the dataset to one machine's lifecycle and caps capacity at that disk
CORRECT
Pays memory prices for cold bulk data that is only streamed during training
Uses a transactional store for bulk blobs, which is costly and ill-suited

stem: Staging and production have quietly diverged after months of manual console edits. The durable fix is:
options: Write a runbook documenting each console step operators are to follow
Define both environments as version-controlled infrastructure-as-code
Grant console access to fewer engineers so fewer manual edits can happen
Snapshot production nightly and restore that image over staging weekly
rationale: Infrastructure-as-code makes the environment definition a reviewed, reproducible artifact, so both environments are provisioned from one source of truth rather than by hand.
misconceptions: Documents a manual process rather than removing the manual process
CORRECT
Reduces who can cause drift but leaves the environment undefined and manual
Copies state periodically without capturing intent, so drift resumes at once

stem: Which approach most directly reduces LLM inference cost and latency at scale?
options: Increase the maximum output token limit so each response finishes in one call
Cache repeats, batch requests, and route simple queries to a smaller model
Raise the sampling temperature so the model commits to its answers sooner
Send every request to the largest model, cutting retries caused by errors
rationale: Caching removes duplicate work, batching raises hardware efficiency, and routing easy traffic to cheaper models cuts per-request cost — all without changing the hard requests.
misconceptions: Raises a cap that permits longer, slower, more expensive generations
CORRECT
Confuses a sampling parameter with anything affecting cost or speed
Maximizes per-request cost on the assumption that errors dominate the bill

stem: A team quantizes a model to int8: memory use halves, but inference latency is essentially unchanged. The most likely reason is:
options: The runtime dequantizes to float for compute, so kernel work is unchanged
Int8 weights occupy more registers, which cancels out the memory savings
Batch size must be doubled before any of the quantization gains appear
Quantization only shrinks the artifact on disk and never the loaded weights
rationale: Without true int8 kernels the runtime unpacks weights back to float before the matmul, so quantization buys memory footprint but no arithmetic speedup.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Invents a register-pressure effect that contradicts the observed halving
Invents a batching precondition for quantization's arithmetic benefits
Contradicts the stated observation that runtime memory use actually halved

stem: Widening the server's dynamic batching window raises GPU throughput, yet user complaints about slowness increase. The most likely explanation is:
options: Larger batches add queueing wait, so per-request tail latency gets worse
Larger batches force the model weights to be reloaded between each batch
Larger batches lower arithmetic precision, so the answers become less useful
Larger batches reduce GPU utilization, so each request is computed slower
rationale: A wider batching window makes early arrivals wait for the batch to fill, trading per-request latency for aggregate throughput — the classic batching trade-off.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Invents weight reloading, which does not depend on batch composition
Confuses batching with quantization; batch size does not change precision
Contradicts the premise that throughput and thus utilization went up

stem: How should database credentials and API keys be handled for a deployed service?
options: Injected at runtime from a secrets manager and never committed to Git
Committed to the repository so that every deployment stays reproducible
Baked into the container image so the service starts without extra config
Printed at start-up so that on-call engineers can confirm the values
rationale: Secrets belong outside the artifact and outside version control, supplied at runtime from a managed store so they can be rotated and access-audited.
misconceptions: CORRECT
Puts secrets in permanent, widely-readable history that cannot be rotated
Bakes secrets into a distributable artifact that anyone pulling it can read
Leaks secrets into logs, which are broadly readable and long-retained

stem: A batch job needs to read objects from exactly one storage bucket. Which grant follows least privilege?
options: Administrator access to the storage service, held only while the job runs
Read-only access scoped to that single bucket, via a role owned by the job
Read-write access to every bucket in the account, granted to the job's role
The team's shared personal credentials, which already carry the needed read
rationale: Least privilege grants exactly the actions on exactly the resources the workload needs — read-only on one bucket, through the job's own identity.
misconceptions: Assumes a time limit substitutes for narrowing permissions themselves
CORRECT
Widens both the action set and the resource scope far beyond the need
Reuses human identities, destroying attribution and over-granting access

stem: Your service logs full request payloads to debug LLM outputs, and users routinely submit personal data. The correct control is:
options: Sample only ten percent of payloads so most personal data is never stored
Keep whole payloads but restrict the log dashboard to the on-call rotation
Encrypt the log volume at rest, which removes the need to redact anything
Redact or hash personal fields before logging, with a retention limit set
rationale: Data minimization at write time is the control: personal data that is never written cannot leak, and a retention limit bounds what does exist.
misconceptions: Reduces the volume of exposure but still stores real personal data indefinitely
Relies on access control while the sensitive data is still collected and kept
Confuses at-rest encryption with minimizing what is collected in the first place
CORRECT
